title: Does self-compassion alter the cortical activity in M1 vs. DLPFC in response to experimentally induced tonic pain?
summary:
Self-compassion — that is, treating oneself with support and understanding — is associated with reduced pain-related distress. Early studies suggest that self-compassionate thoughts may influence how the brain processes pain and how the body responds to stress, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet well understood.
This study examines whether a brief self-compassion exercise alters the perception of cold-induced pain. It also investigates how such an exercise affects bodily reactions, such as heart rate, and the activity of specific brain regions.

Healthy adults take part in the study. Each person attends two sessions. At the first session, participants read neutral, non-emotional sentences before placing their hand on a very cold metal plate for several minutes. During this time, their pain perception, heart rate, and brain activity are recorded. At the second session, the same procedure is repeated — with one difference: before the cold stimulus, participants read sentences that express self-compassion and provide emotional comfort. The cold stimulus and all measurements then follow as before. About one month passes between the two sessions to reduce habituation and account for natural bodily fluctuations.

interventions.name: Healthy participants first complete psychological questionnaires, and their perception of cold pain is then assessed using TMS–EEG, heart rate measurements, and subjective rating scales.
After four weeks, a follow-up assessment is conducted, differing from Arm 1 by including a psychological manipulation using self-compassionate statements prior to the pain stimuli.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Healthy adults
Righthandedness
No acute or chronic pain
Ability to provide informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Current or past psychiatric illnesses
Neurological or cardiac diseases (including epilepsy)
Pregnancy or lactation
Psychoactive medication or substance abuse
Metal implants or electronic implants in the head area
Repeated or unexplained loss of consciousness
